title: Wayfinder: a map of decisions, worked one session at a time
lead: You have a piece of planning too big for one session, and you cannot yet see all of it.
produces: A map of decision tickets worked one at a time until nothing is left to decide, and from it a specification for the whole piece of work. The map settles questions and builds nothing.
scenario: The assay team wants every assay's results out of spreadsheets and into one results store, across three instruments and two sites, with some studies regulated. Run comparison v1, specified in the previous guide, is one small piece of that. It counts as a settled input to this map, not a ticket on it.
input: We want every assay's results out of spreadsheets and into one results store: three instruments, two sites, some studies regulated. Too big to plan at once. Chart it.

steps.label: Name the destination, then list what is open
steps.text: The interview first pins down where this ends. Here it is a specification for the shared results store and the order assays move in. A specification, not software. Then it goes wide instead of deep and lists the open decisions without settling any. If everything fits in one session, it stops and asks how you want to proceed instead of making a map.

steps.label: Chart the map
steps.text: One page holds the destination, a line per decided question, the fog and what is out of scope. The Run comparison v1 specification goes in as input: its decisions, such as one designated reference run per protocol version, are taken as given and not reopened. Each question that can be stated sharply becomes a ticket of one of four types. Grilling and prototype need you, research can be run by an agent, and a task is an errand someone does. Blocking links go in on a second pass. Charting settles nothing by hand, though it starts an agent on each research ticket, and then it stops. Here it yields five tickets and two patches of fog, and building the store is ruled out of scope.

steps.label: Session 1: do the errand
steps.text: A session claims the ticket before touching it, then does it. This one is a task: collect the export format from every instrument. It is the only type that does something. The finding: instruments A and B export CSV with different column layouts, some site 2 files use a decimal comma, and instrument C has nothing usable.

steps.label: Session 2: one question for you
steps.text: A session takes one grilling ticket and nothing else: which assays move first? Each question comes with a recommended answer. You choose unregulated assays on instruments A and B. The answer goes on the ticket, the ticket closes and one line goes on the map. The retirement question, which waited on this, is now answerable. A research ticket can run the same day, because an agent can answer it without you.

steps.label: Redraw after every ticket
steps.text: Each answer can change the map. The research finding, that comparable labs version the plate layout separately, exposes a question nobody could state before: how are plate layouts versioned? The collected exports expose another: which decimal and unit conventions apply across sites? Choosing the first assays exposes a third: who may designate a reference run? It also makes the audit trail for regulated studies sharp enough to ask, so that patch of fog becomes a ticket. It waits for the retirement rule. Failed-run retention stays fog, because nobody can yet say what the question is. A ticket an answer has made pointless is fixed or dropped. Sessions may overlap, so the map is re-read before each one.

steps.label: Session 3: react to something rough
steps.text: Some questions are easier to answer by looking. A throwaway run page takes an hour to sketch. You react: run name, protocol version and reference run at the top, the plate overlay in the middle, flagged wells listed beside it. Only the decision goes into the real work. The sketch stays on a throwaway branch, linked from the ticket.

steps.label: Read the map again
steps.text: The two pictures below are the same map after session 1 and after session 3. Four questions are settled, four are answerable now, one is blocked and one patch of fog remains. The map has grown by four tickets even though three more were closed. The edge of what is known moves as you answer.

steps.label: When nothing is left, write the spec
steps.text: The map is finished when no tickets remain and nothing is left to decide before someone could start the work. Because this map's destination is a specification, it can be written with to-spec from the decided lines on the map, with no new interview. Cutting that specification into build slices is to-tickets, a separate and later choice that the map does not make for you.

steps.label: The specification
steps.text: A document that carries the decisions from the map, the options rejected and the questions deliberately left out.

steps.label: Whether to build, and in what order
steps.text: The map ends at a specification. Whether anyone builds the store, how it is sliced and who builds it are separate decisions made afterwards.

plates.caption: The same map at two points. A square is settled, a pill is answerable now, a rounded box is blocked and a diamond is fog. A solid arrow means one question blocks another or feeds it. A dashed arrow means an answer exposed a new question. The Run comparison v1 specification is an input, not a ticket.

compare.title: A decision map is not a build graph
compare.lead: Both are graphs with blocking links and a frontier, so they get mixed up. They hold different things and end in different places.

rows.decision_map: A question to answer, such as who may designate a reference run. Grilling, research, prototype, or a task that unblocks one.
rows.build_graph: A slice of working software that does something end to end, such as importing an instrument A export.

rows.decision_map: Found as you go. Answers expose new questions, so the graph is partial and grows.
rows.build_graph: Drafted in full before work starts and approved.

rows.decision_map: You cannot ask this well until that is answered. Retiring a reference run waits for which assays move first.
rows.build_graph: This slice cannot start until that one is built. Comparing with the reference run waits for the imports and normalisation.

rows.decision_map: In a specification, when nothing is left to decide.
rows.build_graph: In code that has been checked.

rows.decision_map: That the way is clear. It does not say who builds what, or in what order.
rows.build_graph: That each slice was built and checked on its own.

compare.note: A resolved map leads to to-spec: the specification is written from the decisions on the map. Cutting that specification into build slices is to-tickets, and whether to do it at all is a separate, later choice. The next guide takes that step with Run comparison v1. The reverse also happens: a slice that turns out to hide a question goes back to a map, not to the builder.

plates.caption: The decision map ends in a specification and has fog while it is being worked. The build graph ends in checked code and every slice is known at the start.

artifact.title: Specification excerpt: shared results store
lines: Problem. Results from three instruments at two sites live in spreadsheets, and every comparison is rebuilt by hand.
Solution. One results store. Unregulated assays on instruments A and B move first. Run comparison v1 is its first consumer.
Decision. Each protocol version has one designated reference run. Source: the Run comparison v1 specification and the research ticket.
Decision. The run page shows run, protocol version and reference run at the top, the overlay, and flagged wells beside it.

Open. Reference run retirement, plate layout versioning, decimal and unit conventions, who may designate a reference run, the audit trail and retention of failed runs are not decided, so this excerpt is not final.
Out of scope. Building the store. Instrument C.

stop: You are done charting when the destination is named and the first tickets exist. You are done working when no tickets remain and nothing is left to decide before the work could start. Do not stop because you are tired of the map: remaining tickets are the plan.
limits: One ticket per session is a deliberate rule, so a map is slow by design. Research can run in parallel, but a question that needs you cannot be delegated. A map settles decisions only. It does not show the store can be built or that the decisions are right.
